claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially forms a single-phase, disordered BCC state at high temperature.
The phase stability of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed primarily by the temperature-dependent Gibbs free-energy difference between BCC and FCC.
Kinetic effects modulate the rate at which the alloy approaches its thermodynamically preferred phase state.
Slow cooling permits a near-equilibrium BCC-to-FCC transformation.
Rapid quenching kinetically freezes the high-temperature BCC state.
The alloy is fully BCC above 1000 °C.
Mechanical deformation can trigger a martensitic transformation.
The relevant structural mediator is atomic rearrangement at interfaces between metastable BCC and emerging FCC regions.
As temperature decreases, ΔG_bcc-fcc becomes increasingly negative and makes FCC more thermodynamically favorable than BCC.
Cooling drives a martensitic transformation from BCC to FCC.
Inherently sluggish diffusion in this multicomponent alloy delays the proposed transformation.
Providing more time through slow cooling allows the transformation to proceed despite sluggish diffusion.
Deformation promotes the transformation by introducing nucleation sites.
Slowly cooled or deformed samples will exhibit an increased FCC phase fraction as temperature decreases.
Rapidly quenched samples will mostly retain BCC.
Measured phase fraction should correlate with calculated ΔG_bcc-fcc over the tested temperature range.
The mechanism applies below a thermodynamically calculated critical temperature when the free-energy difference is appreciable and kinetic limitations remain important.
The quantitative ΔG_bcc-fcc threshold, secondary-phase effects, and kinetic barriers for this alloy are not established.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts a low-temperature BCC-to-FCC transformation and increasing FCC fraction, whereas both cited records concern thermodynamic stabilization and deformation-induced transformation in the opposite FCC-to-BCC direction.

The transformation is labeled martensitic, but it is simultaneously explained as being delayed by sluggish diffusion and enabled by extra time for near-equilibrium atomic rearrangement. A martensitic transformation is ordinarily treated as diffusionless, so the diffusional and martensitic pathways are not clearly distinguished.
